1.m: Now, the nine [sounds] from the beginning are the simple vowels.
Two by two, short and long, are homogeneous.
The first twenty-five are the stops.
The subsequent four are the semivowels.
Of the stops in order, [there are] five consonant classes of five each.
[Designated as] first, second, third, fourth, and last.
The spirants, the visarjanīya, and the first and second [stops of each consonant class] are unvoiced.
The remainder of the consonants is voiced.
ā, pra, ava, upa, abhi, adhi, prati, pari, vi, and ni are verbal prefixes.
A speech sound followed by -kāra is the name of that speech sound.
Interposed with the sound a in the case of consonants.
Not for the visarjanīya, jihvāmūlīya, upadhmānīya, anusvāra, and nasal sounds.
A short [vowel] followed by the word varṇa is [the name] of three [forms: short, long, protracted].
The sound aḥ is used for augments, sounds undergoing modification, and sounds undergoing elision.
The first [stop] followed by -varga is the name of the consonant class.
And a vowel of equal duration to it [is short].
A consonant has the duration of half a short [vowel].
Its beginning, as far as half a short [vowel's duration], is higher than the acute, immediately following it.
Or what immediately follows is lower.
Its beginning is equal to the acute, and its remainder is equal to the grave, say the teachers.
The dividable word is treated like separate words when not in a compound enumeration.
Its prior member is the avagraha.
In designations of words, the word [as such] should be understood.
A word consisting of a single speech sound is a single-sound morpheme.
An adjunct, however, constantly marks the position.
And a cause belonging to another word operates in the cases of pragṛhya, srā, and the like.
Repetition is as stated, beginning with three words, beginning with three words.

2.m: [Sound is produced] at the junction of the throat and chest through the propulsion of bodily breath.

2.s: tasya prātiśrutkāni bhavantyuraḥ kaṇṭhaḥ śiro mukhaṃ nāsike iti //
2.d: तस्य प्रातिश्रुत्कानि भवन्त्युरः कण्ठः शिरो मुखं नासिके इति ॥
2.m: Its resonance chambers are the chest, the throat, the head, the mouth, and the nostrils.
When the throat is constricted, voice is produced.
Voice is the mode of phonation in vowels and voiced [consonants].
It is greater in the others than in the first [stops].
In the a-sound, the lips and jaws are neither brought too close together nor drawn too far apart.
The two lips, however, are brought closer together.
And with the middle edges of the tongue one touches the upper molars.
And [the jaws being] brought closer together, one draws the tip of the tongue close to the tooth-sockets in the sounds ṛ, ṝ, and ḷ.
According to some [teachers], also in the anusvāra and the vocalic fragment.
Unless otherwise specified, the tongue is laid flat.
In the i-sound, the middle of the tongue [approaches] the palate.
In the u-sound, there is bringing together of the lips.
Everywhere, however, [it is] by one degree more than the base sound.
Half an a-sound is the beginning of ai and au.
According to some, [it has] a more constricted active articulator.
An i-sound of one and a half [moras] is the remainder of the former.
The anusvāra and the class-finals are nasalised.
Where approximation takes place in vowels, that is the place of articulation.
What brings [them] together is the active articulator.
For other [sounds], however, where contact occurs, that is the place of articulation.
That by which one produces contact is the active articulator.
In the ka-class, one makes contact at the base of the jaws with the root of the tongue.
In the ca-class, [one makes contact] on the palate with the middle of the tongue.
In the ṭa-class, [one makes contact] on the roof of the palate after curling back the tip of the tongue.
In the ta-class, [one makes contact] with the tip of the tongue at the roots of the teeth.
In the sound y, [one makes contact] on the palate with the edges of the middle of the tongue.
In the sound r, [one makes contact] behind the roots of the teeth with the middle of the tip of the tongue.
In the sound v, [one makes contact] with the teeth at the edges of the lips.
The spirants belong in the places of articulation of the stops in regular order.
The middle of the active articulator, however, is open.
The sound h and the visarjanīya have the throat as place of articulation.
According to some [teachers], the sound h has the same place of articulation as the beginning of the following vowel.
The visarjanīya has the same place of articulation as the end of the preceding [sound].
Nasal sounds have the nose as their place of articulation.
Nasalisation arises from opening the nose; nasalisation arises from opening the nose.

3.m: Now, in the subsequent division at the beginning, [a final vowel is] short when followed by a consonant:
devā, śīkā, sumnā, śvartā, vayunā, hṛdayā, agha, ukthā, śuddhā;
prasthā, indriyā, draviṇā, viśvadevyā, dīrghā, vīryā, viśvā, vātā, tvā, bhaṅgurā, karṇakā, vṛṣṇiyā, sugopā, ṛkasāmā, aghā, satrā, varṣā, puṣpā, meghā, prā, svā;

[and in] śaktī, rathī, tviṣī, vāśī, rātrī, oṣadhī, āhutī, vyāhṛtī, svāhākṛtī, hrādunī, śacī, citī, śroṇī, pṛṣṭī, pūtī, abhī, carṣaṇī, paryadhī, pārī, śatrū, viṣū, vasū, anū, hanū, sū, and vibhū, there is avagraha.

[The vowels are lengthened in] avā, sacasvā, nudā, mṛḍā, vardhā, śikṣā, rakṣā, dyā, bhavā, bhajā, yatrā, carā, pibā, nādhā, mādhārayā, dharṣā, ghā, vardhayā, bodhā, trā, tatrā, muñcā, śvasyā, pṛṇasvā, hiṣṭhā, tvaṃ, tarā, janiṣvā, yakṣvā, [and] chā;

kutrā, dakṣiṇenā, svenā, hantanā, jagāmā, ruhemā, vidmardhyāmā, cakṛmā, kṣāmā, starīmā, bharemā, varṣayathā, īrayathā, rithā, pāthā, thā, siñcathā, janayathā, jayathā, ukṣatā, avatā, yātā, śṛṇutā, kṛṇutā, [and] bibhṛtā;
attā, bhavatā, nadatā, taratā, tapatā, juhutā, vocatā, muñcatā, cṛtā, ghuṣyā, janayā, vartayā, sādayā, pārayā, dīyā, harā, bharā, pāsasādā, sṛjā, tiṣṭhā, [and] yenā;
[and] a grave ā preceded by vi and ud, before a non-spirant, before a non-spirant.

4.m: The sound o, not combined [in continuous text], when followed by a consonant that has a short a, [is pragṛhya],
and [also when] preceded by sa, mahat, atha, or pitṛ.

4.s: devate- ubhe- bhāgadhe- ūrdhve- viśākhe- śṛṅge- ene- medhye- tṛṇṇe- tṛdye- kanīnike- pārśve- śive- cottame- evottare- śipre- rathaṃtare- vatsarasyarūpe- virūpe- viṣurūpe- sadohavirdhāne- adhiṣavaṇe- ahorātre- dhṛtavrate- stutaśastre- ṛksāme- aktearpite- raivate- pūrte- pratte- vidhṛte- anṛte- achidre- bahule- pūrvaje- kṛṇudhvam̐sadane //
4.d: देवते- उभे- भागधे- ऊर्ध्वे- विशाखे- शृङ्गे- एने- मेध्ये- तृण्णे- तृद्ये- कनीनिके- पार्श्वे- शिवे- चोत्तमे- एवोत्तरे- शिप्रे- रथंतरे- वत्सरस्यरूपे- विरूपे- विषुरूपे- सदोहविर्धाने- अधिषवणे- अहोरात्रे- धृतव्रते- स्तुतशस्त्रे- ऋक्सामे- अक्तेअर्पिते- रैवते- पूर्ते- प्रत्ते- विधृते- अनृते- अछिद्रे- बहुले- पूर्वजे- कृणुध्वम्̐सदने ॥
4.m: devate, ubhe, bhāgadhe, ūrdhve, viśākhe, śṛṅge, ene, medhye, tṛṇṇe, tṛdye, kanīnike, pārśve, śive and uttame, evottare, śipre, rathaṃtare, vatsarasya rūpe, virūpe, viṣurūpe, sadohavirdhāne, adhiṣavaṇe, ahorātre, dhṛtavrate, stutaśastre, ṛksāme, aktearpite, raivate, pūrte, pratte, vidhṛte, anṛte, achidre, bahule, pūrvaje, [and] kṛṇudhvaṃ sadane;

4.s: amī- cakṣuṣī- kārṣṇī- devatāphalgunī- muṣṭī- dhī- nābhī- vapāśrapaṇī- ahanī- janmanī- sumninī- sāmanī- vaiṣṇavī- aikṣavī- darvī- dyāvāpṛthivī //
4.d: अमी- चक्षुषी- कार्ष्णी- देवताफल्गुनी- मुष्टी- धी- नाभी- वपाश्रपणी- अहनी- जन्मनी- सुम्निनी- सामनी- वैष्णवी- ऐक्षवी- दर्वी- द्यावापृथिवी ॥
4.m: amī, cakṣuṣī, kārṣṇī, devatāphalgunī, muṣṭī, dhī, nābhī, vapāśrapaṇī, ahanī, janmanī, sumninī, sāmanī, vaiṣṇavī, aikṣavī, darvī, [and] dyāvāpṛthivī;
harī, sahurī, sahūtī, kalpayantī, āpṛṣatī, [and] āhutī;
ye aprathetām, urvī, te asya, yaṃ krandasī, chandasvatī, te ācarantī, [and in these words occurring] between them;
the one following ime, garbham, upa, eva, [and] rasena;
and [the one following] krūram, āpaḥ, sajūḥ, [and] brahmajā;
when followed by vīḍ, dvārau, kṛṣṇaḥ, carāvaḥ, or yadā;
but the endings te and the of a polysyllabic word, when preceded by the sound ā or e, [are pragṛhya];
[nor] when followed by te, mā, pātam, namaḥ, enam, abhi, vāyuḥ, garbham, upāha, or stu;
[nor] when followed by ete, tanvau, vau, vā, sam, eva, hi, yajñapadi, or iṣṭakāḥ;

following from ū after gamayataḥ and bhavataḥ, the words from tanū yad akarot, kuryāt, iṣṭiṣu, abrūtām, pravartāḥ, tām, stabhnītām, vācayati, bibhṛtaḥ, tā, agnim, gāyatram, tābhyām eva, ubhābhyām, [and] avāntaram up to the sixth [are pragṛhya].
[The modification does] not [occur before] grāmī, varcasī, mithunī, māse, loke, [and] dhatte.
Constantly before ate in the same word, and before ave and ave.

5.m: Now [the rules] in continuous text, in the case of single-breath utterance.
The operation applies to that which is fitted; that is the original form.
Therein, the preceding [sound undergoes the operation] first, in each case.
Following trapu- and mithu-, the speech sound ś preceded [by them] and followed by c [is inserted].
And [ś is inserted] preceded by su- and followed by candra-.
The speech sound s preceded by sam- and followed by kuru- [is inserted].
And after [the word] akurva, following the affix [s is inserted].
The speech sound d preceded by nīcā- and followed by uccā- [is inserted].

5.s: avagraha āśīrdhūḥsuvariti rephaṃ paraḥ sakāraḥ ṣakāram //
5.d: अवग्रह आशीर्धूःसुवरिति रेफं परः सकारः षकारम् ॥
5.m: In an avagraha, following āśīḥ, dhūḥ, [and] suvaḥ, [visarjanīya becomes] r; following [them], the speech sound s [becomes] ṣ.
Preceded by tu and nu, when both are acute, the speech sound v [is elided].
The speech sound s preceded by ud- and followed by a consonant [is elided].
Sa followed by id, vid, agne, imām, na, enā, [and] oṣadhīḥ [loses its s].
[The s is elided] preceded by sa in tiṣṭhanty ekayā.
The speech sound n followed by c [becomes] the speech sound ś.
[Except in] na, ayan, nairayan, nārdhnuvan, anaḍvān, ghṛṇīvān, vāruṇān, evāsmin.
The speech sound t followed by ś, c, [or] ch becomes c.
The speech sound m followed by a stop [becomes] the nasal sound sharing its place of articulation.
And followed by a semivowel, [it becomes] a nasalised homorganic sound.
And followed by y or v, according to some teachers.
Before the occurrence of the nasal stop or l, the preceding [vowel becomes] nasalised, according to Ātreya.
The speech sound k preceded by a consonant class nasal and followed by s or ṣ [is inserted].
And the speech sound t preceded by ṭ or n [is inserted before s or ṣ].
Preceded by a stop, the speech sound ś becomes ch.
And [not] when preceded by the speech sound p, according to Vālmīki.
Followed by a consonant, according to Pauṣkarasādi; and the preceding [stop becomes] ñ.
Preceded by a first [stop], the speech sound h becomes the fourth [stop] sharing its place of articulation, according to Plākṣi, Kauṇḍinya, Gautama, and Pauṣkarasādi.
[It becomes] the fourth [stop] intermediate between them, according to Śaityāyana and others.
And according to the Mīmāṃsakas, and according to the Mīmāṃsakas.

6.m: Now the speech sound s and visarjanīya become ṣ.
Preceded by svānāsaḥ, divi, ā, pra, u, hi, ayam, u, kam, ūm, u, pra, u, trī, mahi, dyavi, padi, yava, yaḥ, [and] aha-.
Preceded by a verbal prefix ending in i or u, in a grave word.
[Visarjanīya] followed by the speech sound t constantly [becomes s] in rāsaḥ, sapte, agniḥ, nirviduḥ, mīḍhuḥ, pāyubhiḥ, veḥ, sumatiḥ, mākiḥ, īyuḥ, āyuḥ, ābhiḥ, sadhiḥ, [and] nakiḥ.
Preceded by a sound of the a-class, a consonant, śakuni-, patnī-, ṛtu-, mṛtyu-, malimlu-, [and] bṛhaspati-.
[Not in] saṃtānebhyaḥ, saptābhiḥ, saṃmitām, stanām, sītam, spaśaḥ, sak, sani, saniḥ, sanīḥ, sabheyaḥ, sattvā, [and] sasyāyai.
Not [when s is followed by t] preceded by svara-, spardhā-, starī-, masā-, sahasra-, sārathi-, sphurantī-, stub-, jyotiḥ-, āyuḥ-, [and] catuḥ-.

[The original unvoiced spirant] followed by the speech sound t constantly [remains] original s in tarhān, tasmin, lokān, vidvān, tān, trīn, yuṣmān, ūrdhvān, ambakān, ṛtūn, aśman, kṛṇvan, pitṝn, anān, kapālān, tiṣṭhan, in an initially acute word, nemiḥ, devān, savane, [and] paśūn; [it remains] original s constantly.

7.m: Preceded by ṣu, ṣū, kṛdhi, suvaḥ, sam, indrā, sthūri, uru, vāḥ, ṣaṭ, tri, grāma, [and] niṣ-.
en: preceded by parī, pari, parī, and pra.
And in vāhana, uhyamāna, uyāna, mayan, yavena, and vañca.
In indraḥ, when preceded by non-Yajus [matter], with enam and kena.
And the [sound] an in aṅgānām, onegāni, gānām, gyāni, and yāmena.
The [sound] h preceded by r or ṣ in havanya, ahne, and han.
In nahyati, nūnam, nṛtyanti, anyaḥ, anyābhiḥ, anyān, and yantaścāntaśca.

8.m: When followed by the final [sound of a class, it becomes] the final [sound] of its own class.
When followed by a vowel or a voiced [sound, it becomes] the third [sound of its own class].

[Namely, the visarjanīya of] hvār, abhār, vār, hār, abibhar, ajīgar, akar, anantar, vivaḥ, suvaḥ, punar, ahar, ahaḥ, prātar, vastaḥ, śamitaḥ, samitaḥ, sanutaḥ, tanutaḥ, stotaḥ, hotaḥ, pitaḥ, mātaḥ, yaṣṭaḥ, reṣṭaḥ, neṣṭaḥ, and tvaṣṭaḥ.
ahar, ahaḥ, and suvar, when they do not end in the avagraha.
But when preceded by a sound other than an a-sound, [a visarjanīya] followed by r is elided;
According to Uttamottarīya, the two [become] r.
When followed by k, kh, or p, [the visarjanīya] preceded by a sound other than an a-sound [becomes] ṣ within a word [marked with] avagraha;
[and also in] āviḥ, niḥ, iḍaḥ, śaśvataḥ, apasaḥ, deva, riṣaḥ, aṃhasaḥ, ati, divaḥ, viśvataḥ, aśmanaḥ, [and] tamasaḥ,
when followed by kṛdhi, pinva, or pathe.
When followed by patnīva, patī, pate, pataye, patis, or patim.
[In] divaḥ and sahasaḥ when followed by pari or put-.
Not in adhvaram, viśvataḥ, antar, jātaḥ, viviśuḥ, paruḥ, [or] punaḥ;

9.m: According to Kāṇḍamāyana, [the visarjanīya] followed by a spirant is elided before an unvoiced sound.
When followed by an unvoiced sound, [it becomes] the spirant of the same place of articulation as that [following sound].
And when followed by the k-class or p-class, according to Agniveśya and Vālmīki.
Only when followed by a spirant, according to some teachers.
Not according to Plākṣi and Plākṣāyaṇa.
Every [visarjanīya] preceded by a followed by the sound a [becomes] the sound o;
But [a visarjanīya] preceded by an a-sound is elided [before vowels other than a].
Now, when followed by a vowel, [it becomes] y.
The single-sound morpheme u remains unchanged; [the speech sound] v is inserted between [it and the following vowel].
[The speech sound] ṅ preceded by a short [vowel] becomes doubled.
When not followed by iti, in the graha, ukhya, yājyā, pṛṣṭhya, and hiraṇyavarṇīya [sections], [the speech sound n] preceded by ī or u becomes r, and preceded by ā it becomes y,

in martyān, udayān, amṛtān, duryān, preceded by asoma, so, asmān, avimān, gomān, madhumān, haviṣmān, hūtamān; in the ṛṣi [passage]: cikitvān, iḍāvān, kakṣīvān, bāṇavān, hipayasvān, vaśān, vidatrān, amitrān, arān, poṣān, and mahān;
when followed by indro, me, akar, ūrdhvam, iha, apyetu, agan, meḍenyān, āyajiṣṭhaḥ, ācartu, akurvata, aduhata, aditiḥ, agre, adharān, sapatnān, and alam;
not in raśmīn, śrapayān, yamān, pataṅgān, samānān, arcān, [or] yajīyān;
and [not] when followed by udathā, and [not] when followed by udathā.

10.m: A long [vowel results] in a simple vowel when followed by a homogeneous sound.
when followed by e or ai, [they become] ai;
when followed by o or au, [they become] au;
at the confluence of a circumflex and a grave, it is circumflex.
Not in the ṛṣi [verses] dhāmā, apāsi, parī, budhniyājyā, [or] pūṣāminant.
Following eṣṭa, reta, nema, anna, odma, noṣṭha, and iva, the following [vowel] is elided.
An i-vowel and an u-vowel become y and v [respectively].
And when these two are acute, the following grave [vowel] becomes circumflex,
However, y and v preceded by an a-vowel are elided.
However, [only] v [is elided] according to Sāṃkṛtya.
When followed by u or au, they are elided according to Mācākīya.
According to Vātsapra, there is a subtle trace of these two.

11.m: However, the speech sound a preceded by e or o is elided.

In the dhātā, rāti, upa, vājapeya, juṣṭa, śyena, ukhya, dhruvakṣiti, iyam eva sā, agnirmūrdhā, rudra, the first [hymn], the penultimate [hymn], vikarṣa, vihavya, and hiraṇyavarṇīya yājyās of the Mahāpṛṣṭhya;
[before] aṃhasaḥ, aṃhatiḥ, aniṣṭṛtaḥ, avantu, asmān, avadyāt, and in ahani;
preceded by anu gharmāsaḥ, āpaḥ, martaḥ, rathaḥ, tvadattaḥ, vātaḥ;
preceded by āpaḥ, before adbhiḥ, apāṃ napāt, asmān;
preceded by rāye, sa, indraḥ, and when followed by ā;
preceded by te, before adya, andhaḥ, aṃśuḥ, agne;
preceded by naḥ, before asat, agniḥ, aghāt, tamaḥ, abhi, asmin, adya, pathi;
preceded by namaḥ, before agre, aśvebhyaḥ, agriyāya;
preceded by āvinnaḥ somaḥ, when followed by agni;

preceded by dhīrāsaḥ, adabdhāsaḥ, ekādaśāsaḥ, ṛṣīṇāṃ putraḥ, śāryāte, aṣāḍhaḥ, pitāraḥ, pṛthivī, yajñe, āsate, ye, gṛhṇāmi, agre, vām, eṣa, jajñe, saṃsphānaḥ, yuvayoḥ, yaḥ, pṛṣṭhe, patiḥ, vaḥ, gośuṣmaḥ, puvaḥ, samiddhaḥ, ṛṣabhaḥ, pāthaḥ, vacaḥ, varṣiṣṭhe, juṣāṇaḥ, yaḥ, rudraḥ, vṛṣṇaḥ;

[before] aratim, asya yajñasya, atidrutaḥ, atiyanti, anṛṇaḥ, aviṣyan, anamīvaḥ, anneṣu, arciḥ, ajītān, ajyānim, ahniyāḥ, ambāli, arvantam, astu, akṛṇot, aṅgiraḥ, apsu, yaḥ askabhāyat, acyutaḥ, aśvasaniḥ, asthabhiḥ, aśiśret, aṅga, aghniye;
[According to some, the elided a becomes] similar to half of the preceding sound; according to others, similar to half of the preceding sound.

12.m: not when preceded by garbhaḥ, saṃnaddhaḥ, yamaḥ, bhadraḥ;
when followed by y, v, n, h, before vowels;
[and] when followed by j or gna, if acute.
And the preceding [vowel becomes acute when followed by] mo, va, co, dadhāna, sthe;

[and in] abhyāvartin, apūpam, apidadhāmi, adyān, vaditiḥ, śarma, agner jihvām, agnayaḥ, paprayaḥ, asmākam, asme, dhattā, aśmā, aśvā, śrutiḥ, aśyāma, amā, aryaman, asmat, pāśān, asmin yajñe, astā, vyathamānā, abhidroham, adhāyi, adaḥ, atho, adugdhāḥ, ariṣṭāḥ, arathāḥ, arcanti, antarasyām, atra, sthāt, nāya, aṅgirasvat, akaram;
the preceding [vowel becomes acute in] gāhamānaḥ, jāyamānaḥ, hetayaḥ, manyamānaḥ, vanaspatibhyaḥ, pate, sridhaḥ, tapasaḥ, svadhāvaḥ, bhāmitaḥ, agnaye, āyaḥ, adhvaryo, krato.
When that is grave, the preceding acute [becomes] circumflex.
And when an acute follows, a grave [becomes] acute.
And a circumflex everywhere; and a circumflex everywhere.

13.m: And when followed by y or v, according to some teachers.
Preceded by ṛ, ṝ, r, or ṣ, the speech sound n becomes the speech sound ṇ in the same word,
The preceding [speech sound n becomes ṇ] in occurrences of pāṇi, gaṇa, puṇya, kaṇva, kāṇa, gāṇa, bāṇa, veṇu, guṇa, maṇi;
in paṇi, and in the case of paṇiṃvī, yamaṇa, ūṇyāḥ;

[and in] caṅkuṇa, phaṇat, sthūṇau, hiṇuyāt, hiṇoti, kauṇeyaḥ, aṇiṣṭhāḥ, ulbaṇam, ugaṇāḥ, śrutiḥ, cupuṇīkā, bāṇijāya, aṇavaḥ, cāṭṇāra, sthāṇum, tūṇave, vīṇāyām, aśloṇayā, paṇeta, vāṇīḥ, kalyāṇī, kuṇapam, vāṇaḥ, śataśoṇā, śrutiḥ, dhāṇikā, meṇī;
the avagraha [undergoes change to ṇ] in vṛṣaṇ-, śīrṣaṇ-, brahmaṇ-, akṣaṇ-, carmaṇ-, carṣaṇ-;
and ṛṇa, ṣaṇa, ṣṇam, narā, vṇa are original [with ṇ].

13.d: न षुम्नो ऽग्निर्युष्मानीतो ऽन्तो ऽलोपात्स्पर्शपरो व्यवायेषु शसचटतवर्जीयेषु ॥
13.m: Not so in ṣumnaḥ, agniḥ, yuṣmān, ītaḥ, antaḥ, due to non-elision, when followed by a stop, or in intervening sequences excluding ś, s, c, ṭ, and t.
Following a contiguous vowel, l [becomes] ḍ, according to Pauṣkarasādi; according to Pauṣkarasādi.

14.m: Preceded by a vowel and followed by a consonant, a consonant becomes duplicated.
And a stop preceded by l or v [becomes duplicated], according to Pauṣkarasādi.
Only a stop [becomes duplicated], according to some teachers.
but of a second or fourth [consonant] followed by a consonant, the preceding [sound, i.e., the first or third of that class, is introduced];
and always in those preceded by r;
and in ch, kh, [and] bh preceded by a verbal prefix, pātha, eṣa, ati, atī, dhāma, a preceding non-past form of bhū.

14.d: अघोषादूष्मणः परः प्रथमो ऽभिनिधान स्पर्शपरात्तस्य सस्थानः ॥
14.m: Following an unvoiced spirant that is followed by a stop, an abhinidhāna of the first [stop] belonging to the same place of articulation [is inserted];
but after [a spirant] followed by a nasal stop, according to Plākṣāyaṇa.
A first [stop] followed by a spirant becomes a second [stop];
when followed by a [spirant] of a different place of articulation, according to Bāḍabhīkāra.
At a pause: r, visarjanīya, jihvāmūlīya, and upadhmānīya;
and [a spirant] followed by a first [stop], according to Plākṣi and Plākṣāyaṇa;
and the ṭ-class followed by the t-class;
l and the t-class followed by y or v;
when followed by an identical speech sound or a sound of the same class;
a non-nasal stop followed by a nasal stop.
the speech sound l followed by h, ś, or v;
and a word-final original [consonant] followed by a consonant.
A grave following an acute becomes circumflex,
None [becomes circumflex], according to some; none [becomes circumflex], according to some.

15.d: नकारस्य रेफोष्मयकारभावाल्लुप्ते च मलोपाच्च पूर्वस्वरो ऽनुनास्कः ॥
15.m: When the speech sound n becomes r, a spirant, or y, and when it is elided, and upon the elision of m, the preceding vowel becomes nasalised.
and in sṛ and the like, within a single word, when followed by a spirant.
Non-pragṛhya simple vowels are nasalised, according to some [teachers].
And [so is] a word that is protracted, according to Śāṅkhāyana and Kāṇḍamāyana.
The vowel a, however, [is nasalised] even in the continuous text.
Everything has one yama, according to the ancient [teachers]; everything has one yama, according to the ancient [teachers].

16.m: s, r, ś, h, and p, being word-initials, when followed by a vowel, [are followed by s].
And in the forms māsi, māsu, māsaḥ, and māsām.

[And in] hipu, jigā, jighā, chaṃsine, ataṃsayat, ātāṃsīt, kanīyā, jyāyā, drāghīyā, raghīyā, śreyā, hrasīyā, vasīyā, bhūyāṃsaḥ, jakṣivā, jaghnivā, jigivā, jīgivā, tasthivā, dāśvā, dīdivā, papivā, pīpivā, vidvā, viviśivā, śuśruvā, and sasṛvā.
The vowels ā, e, and o, when followed by si or ṣi at word-ends [take anusvāra or nasalisation].
What is not ā [becomes] short, according to Sāṃkṛtya.
Not in a two-vowel word, regularly.
And in ṛjīṣi, jigāsi, jighāsi, ajāsi, yajāsi, dadāsi, dadhāsi, and vartayāsi.
[Anusvāra occurs] after daṃsanābhyaḥ, daṃsobhiḥ, daṃsam, vṛṣadaṃśaḥ, daṃśukā, and daṃṣṭrābhyām.
[And in] maṃsye, maṃsatai, yaṃsat, yaṃsan, vaṃsate, and vaṃsagaḥ.
The diphthong ai, according to Ukhya, is fully nasalised.
[In] śiṃśumāraḥ, śiṃṣat, saṃśvā, saṃsrā, saṃsṛṣṭa, saṃskṛtya, saṃkṛta, saṃśita, saṃśitā, kiṃśila, and kiṃśilā.
Initial [in] aṃhatiḥ, aṃhaḥ, aṃhoḥ, aṃhomuc, aṃtyaṃhāḥ, aṃhasaḥ, aṃhasām, aṃśam, aṃśubhiḥ, aṃśabhuvām, aṃśvam, aṃśū, aṃśavaḥ, aṃśuḥ, aṃśum, aṃśūn, aṃśunā, aṃśoḥ, aṃśāya, upāṃśu, and aṃśau.
With acute avagraha in aṃse, aṃsāya, aṃsābhyām, and aṃsau.

17.m: Nasalisation is more intense in anusvāra and nasal consonants, according to Śaityāyana.
It is the same everywhere, according to Kauhalīputra.
In anusvāra, it is slight, according to Bhāradvāja.

17.s: nākārasya rephoṣmayakārabhāvāllupte ca malopāccottaramuttaraṃ tītrataramiti sthaviraḥ kauṇḍinyaḥ //
17.d: नाकारस्य रेफोष्मयकारभावाल्लुप्ते च मलोपाच्चोत्तरमुत्तरं तीत्रतरमिति स्थविरः कौण्डिन्यः ॥
17.m: From the transformation of n into r, a spirant, or y, and upon elision [of n], and from the elision of m, each subsequent one is more intense, says the elder Kauṇḍinya.
And the consonant duration of the vowel is greater in this case.
In the case of a circumflex and a vikrama, there is firmer effort, according to Pauṣkarasādi.
[This applies] to all speech sounds, because of differences in effort, according to Śaityāyana.

17.s: nātivyaktaṃ na cāvyaktamevaṃ varṇānudiṅgayet / payaḥpūrṇamivāmatram̐ harandhiro yathāmati // ityātreya ātreyaḥ //
17.d: नातिव्यक्तं न चाव्यक्तमेवं वर्णानुदिङ्गयेत् । पयःपूर्णमिवामत्रम्̐ हरन्धिरो यथामति ॥ इत्यात्रेय आत्रेयः ॥
17.m: ‘One should utter speech sounds thus: neither too distinct nor indistinct; / like a resolute man carrying a pot full of milk, according to his ability’—so says Ātreya, so says Ātreya.

18.d: ओकारं तु प्रणव एके ऽर्धतृतीयमात्रं ब्रुवते ॥
18.m: Some, however, declare the vowel o in the praṇava to have a duration of two and a half morae.
[It has] one of acute, grave, or circumflex [tones], according to Śaityāyana.
It has the sustained pracaya tone, according to Kauṇḍinya.
That utterance of speech is [delivered] in the middle register.
It is circumflex, according to Plākṣi and Plākṣāyaṇa.

18.s: yathāprayogaṃ vā sarveṣāṃ yathāprayogaṃ vā sarveṣām //
18.d: यथाप्रयोगं वा सर्वेषां यथाप्रयोगं वा सर्वेषाम् ॥
18.m: Or according to actual practice for all; or according to actual practice for all.

19.s: svaritayormadhye yatra nīcam̐ syādudāttayorvānyatarato vodāttasvaritayoḥ sa vikramaḥ //
19.d: स्वरितयोर्मध्ये यत्र नीचम्̐ स्यादुदात्तयोर्वान्यतरतो वोदात्तस्वरितयोः स विक्रमः ॥
19.m: Where a low [vowel] occurs between two circumflexes, or between two acutes, or between an acute and a circumflex on either side, that is a vikrama.
And preceded by a pracaya, according to Kauṇḍinya.
Some [hold it to have] two yamas; where followed by two yamas, these are an atom of a mora [in duration].
Not in the earlier treatise; not in the earlier treatise.

20.m: When the i-vowels or u-vowels turn into y or v while both are acute, [the resulting circumflex is] the kṣaipra.

20.s: sayakāravakāraṃ tvakṣaraṃ yatra svaryate sthite pade 'nudāttapūrve 'pūrve vā nitya ityeva jānīyāt //
20.d: सयकारवकारं त्वक्षरं यत्र स्वर्यते स्थिते पदे ऽनुदात्तपूर्वे ऽपूर्वे वा नित्य इत्येव जानीयात् ॥
20.m: Where a syllable containing y or v is circumflexed in a fixed word, whether preceded by a grave or not preceded [by a grave], one should know it as the nitya [circumflex].

20.s: api cennānāpadasthamudāttamatha cetsām̐hitena svaryate sa prātihataḥ //
20.d: अपि चेन्नानापदस्थमुदात्तमथ चेत्साम्̐हितेन स्वर्यते स प्रातिहतः ॥
20.m: Even if it is acute when occurring in different words, yet if it is circumflexed in the continuous text, that is the prātihata [circumflex].
When the vowel a is elided after it, [the circumflex is] the abhinihata.
In a hiatus between words, [the circumflex is called] pādavṛtta.
Preceded by an acute [and separated by consonants, it is] tairovyañjana.
In the kṣaipra and nitya, [the downward slide/glide is] firmer.
In the praśliṣṭa and prātihata, it is softer.
In the tairovyañjana and pādavṛtta, it is weaker and weaker.

21.m: The anusvāra and the vocalic fragment [belong to the preceding vowel].
Not [so when the first consonant of a cluster is] followed by a non-homorganic semivowel.
And a stop followed by a spirant, and a spirant if followed [by another consonant, belong to the preceding vowel].
After a circumflex in continuous text, the series of grave [vowels] sounds like an acute.
After a non-final stop followed by a final stop, nasal sounds [arise] in succession.
After h followed by n, ṇ, or m, there is a nasal sound.
In a combination of r and a spirant, there is a vocalic fragment of r.
Not in the kramapāṭha when followed by a first [stop], when followed by a first [stop].

22.m: Sound is the material cause of all speech sounds.
By difference in its form arises difference in speech sounds.
Now we shall set forth the verbal particles.
Tu ('but'), atha ('now'), and eva ('only') indicate, respectively, restriction/exception, heading, and limitation.
Tension, sharpness, and narrowing of the throat produce highness of sound.
Relaxation, softness, and widening of the throat produce lowness.
Low register, middle register, and high register are the places of production.

22.s: ṛgvirāmaḥ padavirāmo vivṛttivirāmaḥ samānapadavivṛttivirāmastrimātro dvimātra ekamātro 'rdhamātra ityānuūrvyeṇa //
22.d: ऋग्विरामः पदविरामो विवृत्तिविरामः समानपदविवृत्तिविरामस्त्रिमात्रो द्विमात्र एकमात्रो ऽर्धमात्र इत्यानुऊर्व्येण ॥
22.m: A verse pause, a word pause, a hiatus pause, and an internal-word hiatus pause are, in order, three morae, two morae, one mora, and half a mora.

22.s: yadyañjanāntaṃ yadu cāpi dīrgham̐ saṃyogapūrvaṃ ca tathānunāsikam // etāni sarvāṇi gurūṇi vidyāc cheṣāṇyato 'nyāni tato laghūni //
22.d: यद्यञ्जनान्तं यदु चापि दीर्घम्̐ संयोगपूर्वं च तथानुनासिकम् ॥ एतानि सर्वाणि गुरूणि विद्याच् छेषाण्यतो ऽन्यानि ततो लघूनि ॥
22.m: What ends in a consonant, what is long, what precedes a consonant cluster, and likewise what is nasalised / one should know all these as heavy; the remaining, other than these, are light.

22.s: avyañjanāntaṃ yaddhrasvamasaṃyogaparaṃ ca yat / ananusvārasaṃyuktametallaghu niṣodhatai tallaghu nibodhata //
22.d: अव्यञ्जनान्तं यद्ध्रस्वमसंयोगपरं च यत् । अननुस्वारसंयुक्तमेतल्लघु निषोधतै तल्लघु निबोधत ॥
22.m: What does not end in a consonant, what is short and not followed by a consonant cluster, / and not combined with anusvāra—understand this to be light, understand that to be light.

23.m: Now [follows] the origin of the distinctions among speech sounds.
"From mode of phonation, contact, place of articulation, disposition of the active articulator, / and fifthly from duration, arises the difference among speech sounds."
Sound articulated into speech sounds is the production of speech.
Whispered, murmured, subdued voice, resonant tone, low register, middle register, and high register.
Whispered is with movement of the articulators, without sound, and without mental projection.
Murmured is without distinct perception of vowels and consonants.

23.s: urasi mandraṃ kaṇṭhe madhyamam̐ śirasi tāram //
23.d: उरसि मन्द्रं कण्ठे मध्यमम्̐ शिरसि तारम् ॥
23.m: Low register is in the chest, middle register in the throat, high register in the head.
In the three places of production beginning with the low register, there are seven notes each.
The kṛṣṭa, the first, the second, the third, the fourth, the mandra, and the atisvārya.
Their perception is born of brightness.
The three—the second, the first, and the kṛṣṭa—are the calling tones.
The four beginning with the mandra and ending with the second belong to the Taittirīyakas.
For the Taittirīyas, the mandra is after the second, and immediately next are the third and fourth; they call that the four-tone [scale].
In that [recitation], the interval consists of two notes.
That has been described as the four-tone [scale].

23.s: kramivakramasaṃpannāmadrutāmavilambitām / nīcoccasvārasaṃpannāṃ vadeddhṛtavatīm̐ samāṃ vadeddhṛtavatīm̐ samāmiti //
23.d: क्रमिवक्रमसंपन्नामद्रुतामविलम्बिताम् । नीचोच्चस्वारसंपन्नां वदेद्धृतवतीम्̐ समां वदेद्धृतवतीम्̐ समामिति ॥
23.m: One should recite smoothly, endowed with step-like progression, neither rushed nor lingering, / endowed with low, high, and circumflex tones, firm and even, firm and even.

24.m: Now there are four continuous texts.
The word continuous text, the syllable continuous text, the speech-sound continuous text, and the member continuous text.
The combination of separate words joined together is called word-continuous text.
In the same way, the continuous text of syllables and so forth [are defined] according to their own nature.

24.s: gurutvaṃ laghutā sāmyam̐ hrasvadīrghaplutāni ca / lopāgamavikārāśca prakṛtirvikramaḥ kramaḥ // svaritodāttanīcatvam̐ śvāso nādo 'ṅgameva ca / etatsarvaṃ tu vijñeyaṃ chandobhāṣāmadhīyatā //
24.d: गुरुत्वं लघुता साम्यम्̐ ह्रस्वदीर्घप्लुतानि च । लोपागमविकाराश्च प्रकृतिर्विक्रमः क्रमः ॥ स्वरितोदात्तनीचत्वम्̐ श्वासो नादो ऽङ्गमेव च । एतत्सर्वं तु विज्ञेयं छन्दोभाषामधीयता ॥
24.m: Heaviness, lightness, equality, and short, long, and protracted [quantities], / elision, augment, and modification, original form, separation, and kramapāṭha, // circumflex, acute, and low pitch, breath, voice, and the limb [of a word]— / all this must indeed be known by one studying the language of the meters.

Knowing the particularities of words and the kramapāṭha, discerning in the sequence of speech sounds, / knowing the division of vowels and moraic measure, he may enter the assembly of teachers—he may enter the assembly of teachers.
